ai.literal: To those who suffer and grieve from love, there is no strength or refuge other than the palmyra-stem horse.
ai.translation: For those who suffer and grieve under the pain of love, there is no other strength or refuge except riding the palmyra-stem horse.
ai.modern: காம நோயால் வருந்தித் துன்பப்படுபவர்களுக்கு, மடலேறுதலைத் தவிர வேறு எந்தப் புகலிடமும் வலிமையும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the desperate state of a lover who is suffering from intense love-sickness. The word 'maṭal' refers to the ancient practice of riding a horse made of jagged palmyra stems to publicly declare one's unrequited love. The poet explains that for those who endure such agonizing love ('kāmam uḻantu varuntinārkku'), there is no other source of strength ('vali') or refuge ('ēmam') left to them. By choosing to ride the 'maṭal', the lover abandons all social modesty as a final, desperate attempt to find relief.

ai.literal: Not enduring body and life will ride the palmyra horse, modesty having cast aside and put away.
ai.translation: My body and life, unable to bear this suffering, will ride the palmyra horse, having completely cast aside and put away all modesty.
ai.modern: துன்பத்தைப் பொறுக்க முடியாத என் உடலும் உயிரும், நாணத்தை நீக்கித் தூரத்தே வைத்துவிட்டு, மடலேறும்.
ai.explanation: The lover expresses the extremity of his grief caused by separation from his beloved. He declares that his body and life can no longer endure the pain, forcing him to resort to 'madalēṟutal'—the public act of riding a horse made of rough palmyra stems to proclaim his love. To take this desperate step, he must completely cast aside ('nīkki') and put away ('niṟuttu') his sense of shame and modesty ('nāṇ'). The couplet illustrates how overwhelming love-sickness overpowers a person's natural restraint and social decorum.

ai.literal: With modesty, good manliness, formerly I possessed; today I possess, those who are in love ride, the palmyra horse.
ai.translation: In the past, I possessed modesty and noble self-control; today, all I possess is the palmyra horse that those consumed by love ride.
ai.modern: முன்பு நான் நாணத்தையும் நல்ல ஆண்மையையும் (மனவலிமையையும்) பெற்றிருந்தேன்; ஆனால் இன்று, காதலில் வருந்துவோர் ஏறும் மடல் குதிரையை மட்டுமே நான் பெற்றுள்ளேன்.
ai.explanation: The hero, suffering from the intense pain of separation and unfulfilled love, speaks of his desperate state. In the past, he was guided by modesty (நாண்) and strong self-control or manliness (ஆண்மை). However, the overwhelming power of his love has stripped him of these virtues. Now, his only possession and recourse is the 'madal' (மடல்)—a horse made of sharp palmyra stems, which disappointed lovers traditionally ride publicly to proclaim their love and seek sympathy.

ai.literal: The fierce flood of passion carries away indeed, along with modesty, the raft called good strength of character.
ai.translation: The fierce flood of desire sweeps away the raft of modesty and strength of character.
ai.modern: காமம் என்னும் கடுமையான வெள்ளம், நாணமும் நல்ல மனவலிமையும் ஆகிய தெப்பத்தை அடித்துச் சென்றுவிடுகிறது.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid metaphor to describe the overwhelming power of desire. The poet compares intense love or passion to a fierce, raging flood (கடும்புனல்). To survive this flood, a person relies on a raft (புணை) constructed of modesty (நாண்) and strong self-control or dignity (ஆண்மை). However, the torrent of passion is so powerful that it sweeps away even this protective raft, leaving the individual helpless against their desires.

ai.literal: She who wears a garland and small bracelets gave [me] the grief that afflicts [me] in the evening, along with [the need to ride] the palmyra-stem horse.
ai.translation: She who wears a flower garland and small bracelets has given me this grief, which afflicts me in the evening, along with the desperate urge to ride the palmyra-stem horse.
ai.modern: மாலை போன்ற மாலையையும் சிறிய வளையல்களையும் அணிந்தவள், எனக்கு மாலைப் பொழுதில் வருத்தும் துன்பத்தையும், அதனுடன் மடல் ஏறும் நிலையையும் தந்துவிட்டாள்.
ai.explanation: In this verse, the hero expresses his intense suffering due to separation from his beloved. He describes her as one wearing a flower garland (தொடலை) and small bracelets (குறுந்தொடி). He laments that she has given him a deep grief (துயர்) that torments him especially during the evening (மாலை). This unbearable sorrow drives him to the extreme step of riding the 'maḍal' (மடல்), a traditional practice where a desperate lover publicly rides a horse made of rough palmyra stems to proclaim his love.

ai.literal: Riding the palmyra horse, even at midnight, I will think of, surely; closing not agreeing, because of the beloved, my eyes.
ai.translation: My eyes refuse to close in sleep because of my beloved; surely, even in the dead of night, I think only of riding the palmyra horse.
ai.modern: என் கண்கள் அந்தப் பேதைக்காகத் தூங்குவதற்கு உடன்படவில்லை; அதனால், நள்ளிரவிலும் நான் மடல் ஊர்வதைப் பற்றியே நிச்சயமாக நினைப்பேன்.
ai.explanation: The lover is suffering from sleeplessness because of his beloved, whom he refers to as 'pētai' (the innocent or simple girl). Since his eyes refuse to close (paṭal ollā) in sleep, he lies awake even during the dead of night (yāmattum). In this quiet, sleepless state, his mind is entirely and surely (maṉṟa) occupied with the thought of riding the palmyra horse (maṭalūrtal) to publicly declare his love and end his torment.

ai.literal: Ocean-like desire even though suffering, palmyra-horse not mounting, than woman, greatly worthy thing there is not.
ai.translation: There is nothing more greatly worthy than a woman who, even though suffering from a desire as vast as the ocean, does not mount the palmyra-horse.
ai.modern: கடல் போன்ற காம நோயால் துன்புற்றாலும், மடலேறாத பெண்ணை விடப் பெருமைக்குரியவர் வேறு யாரும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: In classical Tamil love poetry, a man suffering from intense, unrequited love may threaten to ride a 'maḍal' (a painful horse made of rough palmyra stems) to publicly declare his grief. However, women are expected to maintain their modesty and never resort to this extreme public act. This couplet praises the restraint of women, stating that there is nothing more noble or worthy of respect than a woman who bears a desire as vast as the ocean without ever resorting to mounting the palmyra-horse. Her self-control and adherence to modesty, even under immense emotional suffering, represent the pinnacle of dignity.

ai.literal: Without thinking, 'They have rare self-control, indeed they are pitiable,' love, transgressing secrecy, will appear in the public place.
ai.translation: Without considering, 'These people have rare self-control,' or 'They deserve pity,' love overflows its secrets and exposes itself in public.
ai.modern: இவர்கள் மிகுந்த மனவலிமை உடையவர்கள் என்றும், இவர்கள் இரங்கத்தக்கவர்கள் என்றும் எண்ணாமல், காமமானது தன் இரகசியங்களைக் கடந்து பொதுவெளியில் வெளிப்பட்டுவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes how overwhelming passion cannot be hidden by modesty or self-restraint. The speaker notes that love (kāmam) does not pause to think whether the lovers possess rare self-control (niṟai) or whether they deserve pity (aḷiyar) for their suffering. Instead, it breaks through all barriers of privacy and secrecy (maṟai) and reveals itself openly in public (maṉṟu). The contrast between internal restraint and the unstoppable public manifestation of love highlights the helplessness of the lovers.

ai.literal: They do not know, everyone, thinking thus indeed, my love, in the street, wanders in distress, having become bewildered.
ai.translation: Thinking 'no one knows of my secret', my love has become bewildered and wanders openly in distress in the public street.
ai.modern: எல்லாரும் என் காதலைப் பற்றி அறியவில்லை என்று நினைத்து, என் காமமானது மருட்சியடைந்து தெருவிலே அலமந்து சுழல்கிறது.
ai.explanation: The speaker describes how their intense love, which they tried to keep hidden, has now become public. Believing that no one else knew about this secret passion, the love itself has become bewildered and has spilled out into the public streets. The word 'maruku' has a double meaning: it refers to a public street and also means to be agitated or to whirl in distress. By saying 'marukiṉ marukum' (wanders in distress in the street), the poet brilliantly highlights how a deeply private grief has transformed into a highly visible public exposure.

ai.literal: While we see with our eyes, those who lack understanding laugh, because they themselves have not suffered what we have suffered.
ai.translation: Those who lack understanding laugh at me right before my eyes, only because they themselves have never suffered the pain that I have suffered.
ai.modern: நாங்கள் எங்கள் கண்களால் பார்க்கும்படி, அறிவு இல்லாதவர்கள் எங்களைப் பார்த்துச் சிரிக்கிறார்கள்; நாங்கள் அனுபவித்த துன்பங்களை அவர்கள் அனுபவிக்காத காரணத்தால் தான்.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the lover laments the mockery of the townspeople who do not comprehend the agony of love-sickness. The phrase 'arivillār' refers to these onlookers, whom the lover calls 'lacking in understanding' because they lack empathy. They laugh openly right in front of the lover's eyes ('kaṇṇiṉ kāṇa nakupa'). The lover explains that this ridicule happens only because these people have never themselves experienced ('tām paṭā') the intense suffering ('yām paṭṭa') that the lover is going through.
